demurrage charges and all of the other related expenses that come about as a result of that work problem. I will not call it a stoppage, but it certainly is a problem.
What the Hon. Member for Prince Albert failed to say- and this is why I always wonder why they pose themselves as friends of the farmer-was that every time there is a work stoppage at the Port of Vancouver which stops the flow of grain from the Prairies and there is back to work legislation proposed in the House, since I have been here the New Democrats from the Prairies, who are supposed to be the champions of the farmers, vote against the back to work legislation. While the Hon. Member for Prince Albert is decrying the imposition of those terrible costs on the farmers from the Prairies, his colleagues from the Prairies always support the work stoppage and the increased cost to the prairie farmer.
The Members on my left cannot have it both ways. They either have to be for the farmer in this case or against the farmer. When it comes to voting back to work legislation for a few hundred workers in the Vancouver area, they will vote for the union and against the farmer. They have done it ever since I have come to this House. I fail to see why they have been successful in posing as the friend of the farmer when they actually vote against the farmer whenever there is a confrontation between the farmer and the port workers in Vancouver.
In the few minutes remaining to me, I would like to speak about this very important issue, the Crow rate. It is true that the legislation would do away with the statutory protection for the farmer and provide statutory protection for the railway. That in itself is an inequity that violates the basic sense of fairness that the Canadian people have. It is not fair to continue protection to the railways but to deny it to the farmer.
While inflation and increased costs of production impinge heavily on the farmer, and in the last ten years there has been 135 per cent increase in inflation and the cost of production for the farmer, there is still no protection for the farmer in terms of freight rates. Therefore, I understand the tension that exists on the Prairies when it comes to this legislation.
What bothers me most in the sweetheart deal between the railways and the Government is the double standard that has been invoked. We are arguing a rate that was established 80 years ago. At that time the railways agreed through a statutory limit that they would not charge more than a certain amount for the transport of grain. Today those costs bear no resemblance to the present day costs. The payment established 80 years ago bears no relationship to today's transport costs. We have the railways coming to us and saying they cannot operate under this arrangement because there is no realistic relationship between the cost of 80 years ago and today. I can understand that, but let us examine the language of the railway on another issue, namely, railway pensions.
My friend, the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) indicated this morning the way the railways treat their minority shareholders in terms of stocks and dividends and the way they have robbed minority shareholders over the years by the
June 16, 1983

way they have treated long-term arrangements. The same is true of the workers. If there is one thing that has gratified me over the years, it is the sense of loyalty that I have experienced on the part of railway workers to the railways. CPR and CNR employees are proud of their railways.
No, of the work.

The Hon. Member says of the work, but they are proud of the railways. What bothers me is that in spite of this intense pride those workers have for their work and for their railways, they have been betrayed by the railways. Let me illustrate by way of their pension plans.
There are two pension plans that have been devised by the railways over the years, one covering pensions from 1935 to 1959 and one covering from 1959 to 1967. The pension plan devised for 1935 to 1959 gave the workers a pension of 40 per cent over the best ten years of employment. Let us say that that was a S3 average over 1950 to 1960; 40 per cent of those best ten years. What relationship is there between that payment now and the cost of living for those pensioners? There is no fairness at all.
Some years ago when I wrote to Ian Sinclair of CP Investment about that inequity, he said, "That's tough, they invested that money in long-term arrangements and they have to pay back according to their return on that investment". I have a letter from Mr. Roy Lowry, administrative officer of the president's office of CNR. Listen to the language he uses: "The employees' contribution, subject to matching contributions from the company with interest accrued to date of retirement, represented the company's obligation." When it comes to the employers' or the former employees' obligations, it is all statutory. There is no consideration given to the increased cost of living. There is no consideration given to the inflationary spiral. There is no consideration given to the plight of those former employees who are now living on meagre pensions. It is always a statutory obligation.
Why is it, Mr. Speaker, that the railway can argue so eloquently about changing the statutory regulation when it comes to subsidies for the railway, but it is speechless when it comes to the statutory obligations for the pensioner? Why is it, Mr. Speaker, that it needs so much to operate because of the spiralling costs of production, but it cannot argue on behalf of its employees who are living on a meagre income?
Let me close by saying, Mr. Speaker, that it seems to me that the unions that are supposed to be defending employees have been no better because the unions forget the employees as soon as they are retired. They work for them as long as they are employed, but out of sight means out of mind. In that sense the unions have done no better than management.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-155 today. The Bill has commonly been called the Crow rate Bill and is perhaps
Western Grain Transportation Act
not readily understood in large urban centres such as metropolitan Toronto. Generally speaking, it is viewed as something that concerns only those Canadians who are involved in the farming communities.
They know that it means jobs.

They certainly do know that it means jobs and, apparently, they understand that much better than does the Liberal Party. That is why the farming community is so concerned about the changes that the Government is trying to impose upon them.
My good friend, the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Smith), wondered whether there were any farmers in Beaches who were particularly concerned about the amendments that the Government intends to make to the Crow rate, and I want to assure him that while there are no farmers as they are commonly understood, certainly many of my constituents lived on farms and migrated to the city. These people certainly understand the implications of the Crow rate and they have expressed their concerns to me.
The issue that we in the House are talking about deals not only with individuals who are directly involved in the farm industry. It goes far beyond that. It goes deeper than that. It goes to a basic principle-
It creates many jobs.

I will talk about jobs, and I will also talk about jobs in the Hon. Minister's constituency that will be lost because of what the Government intends to do.
We are actually talking about a social contract between Canadians and their Government which goes back to the 1800s because it was back then, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Pacific Railway received substantial mineral rights, land and cash from the people of Canada in exchange for certain responsibilities. One of those obligations was to haul grain at the Crow rate. Another was to use its mineral resources to keep its transcontinental rail line modern and efficient as the country grew.
Now Canadian Pacific says that it wants to keep the mineral rights and grants but shift its obligations to farmers and taxpayers who will have to pay the bills. The Government agrees with CP and has introduced legislation to end the Crow rates for grain transportation. This action will provoke a deep and possibly desperate reaction on the part of the people on the Prairies who consider the Crow their Confederation bargain.
The Crow is also important to central Canada. If the farmers have to pay higher freight charges, they will have less money to spend on tractors, trucks and supplies made in central Canada. Thousands of workers at farm implement plants in Ontario, for example, are already on lay-off. Doing away with the Crow will guarantee more lost jobs.
As another example, the extra freight charges to be paid by farmers under the Government's plan will lower the Canadian Gross National Product by some $1.5 billion in 1991, which means that the economy will then support some 51,000 fewer jobs than it does today.

June 16, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
Higher freight charges to ship grain in Canada will also divert grain from the Canadian Prairies to U.S. ports. My friend, the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong), has raised this issue in the House during Question Period and has yet to receive a satisfactory response from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). Canadians who work on the railways, the Great Lakes and the Seaway will also lose jobs because of the Government's proposals.
If farmers have to pay higher freight charges, they will produce less grain. Even Agriculture Canada admits that this will mean a reduction in grain exports which now earn our country some $6 billion a year in foreign exchange.
While the New Democratic Party is in favour of upgrading Canadian railways, we would pay the railways for their proven losses hauling grain at the Crow rate and make public investment to upgrade the rails for all commodities in all regions, not just those favoured by the Minister and Canadian Pacific and the other railways. Our proposal would cost no more than the Government's plan but more rail upgrading would be accomplished because we would prevent public money from leaving the rail system and going to dividends or foreign real estate. The taxpayers have paid for rail upgrading for over 100 years, and we say that it is time we stopped the handouts and instead took equity in Canadian Pacific Limited and Canadian National for what we pay.
In 1881, Mr. Speaker, the CPR syndicate accepted from the people of Canada land, cash, rail lines and other benefits in exchange for a commitment to "thereafter and forever efficiently maintain, work and run the Canadian Pacific Railway". Clearly Parliament intended that the vast land grants and other benefits were to permit the syndicate to finance the railway's ongoing operation.
In general terms, the Crow rate is one half of an indivisible national policy dating back to the time of Sir John A. Macdonald that was to provide tariff protection for central industry and low cost transport to develop the eastern and western region. Specifically, the Crow rate was agreed upon by the CPR and the Government of Canada and remains a valid and binding contract. Sir Clifford Sifton, party to the negotiations that established the 1897 Crow rate agreement, said in 1929:
! remember when as a young minister in Laurier's cabinet. Van Horne and Shaughnessy said a line into the Kootenay mining district would not be considered for fifteen years. Also I remember that within six weeks the same two gentlemen came into my office and said that they had to build this line and wanted a large bonus for doing it, that the CPR was on the verge of bankruptcy. We gave them this bonus against the public sentiment of two-thirds of the people of Canada. They built the line and the Kootenay mining development (nucleus of Cominco) saved the CPR and saved a good many other things in Canada.
Again, Mr. Speaker, in 1925, Parliament put the Crow rate in a statute when the railways offered to keep grain on the Crow rate if they could be relieved from the agreement for low rates on other commodities. At the time, the CPR made it clear that they were not asking for any change in the conditions established in 1897 in regard to grain and grain products.
A. R. Gobeil, one member of the MacPherson Royal Commission on Transportation, had this to say:
-the grain rates were not imposed by Parliament. They were not only freely accepted by the railway but were offered by them as an inducement to persuade Parliament to lift that part of the agreement which pertained to westbound rates on other commodities.
At no time in 1925 was there a suggestion by either Party that the agreement of 1897 was being terminated. The Crows-nest Pass Agreement is a binding contract and if the Canadian Pacific Railway wishes to be relieved of its obligation under that agreement, it must also relinquish the other benefits it derives.
I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I urge the Government and all Members on this side of the House to defeat this totally inequitable Bill which will work against Canadian farmers.
Mr. Speaker, today I am speaking on something that I knew absolutely nothing about three weeks ago.

No, big mouth.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Remarks should be addressed to the Chair, as the Hon. Member knows.

Mr. Speaker, because of the importance of this Bill I have had an opportunity to become aware of the Crows-nest Pass rate. To me it is another example of the destruction of our national transportation system. In Ontario we have seen the destruction of the rail passenger service, and indeed that has gone on even beyond Ontario, but in my riding the train that used to go past the back of my property every day no longer operates.
This week I had an opportunity to help a gentleman who found that he could not send his vehicle by train because it was too heavy. He was told the railways did not have the service. Strangely enough, Air Canada came to the rescue; the airline could take it but VIA Rail could not. I spoke to the Minister about that case and he admitted it was strange that the train could not take a large wheelchair vehicle when it had a mail car. That is another example of the Government's attitude towards rail transportation in this country.
It is the historical implications of the Bill that we are dealing with. I support the NDP motion for a six-month hoist. It took us six months to get the Constitution and it should have taken longer. This Bill should go to committee for at least six months so that everyone in the country can discuss it, not just Members of Parliament who have been brought up to date on the matter. This is a sound proposal, Mr. Speaker. There is no reason to rush this. There is no reason that the Transport Committee could not meet throughout the summer to hear the views of people from across the land. I notice that one of my colleagues who is involved in transportation does not like that idea very well, but I would be prepared to sit on that Committee to become more aware of the transportation system in the country.
June 16, 1983

This Party agrees, in principle, to some adjustment but not that set forth by the Minister. We must have some freedom in this country and, as the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) has stated a number of times, what we are pushing for is freedom of choice. The trouble with not having freedom of choice is that it leaves too much power in the hands of Government and the railways while it removes power from the farmers, the producers and processors. 1 feel that the Bill leaves far too much power with the railways and too much with the Minister.
1 should like to compare this subsidy with a few things in Ontario. There are local transportation commissions which are all subsidized by the taxpayer. VIA Rail is subsidized by the taxpayer, the St. Lawrence Seaway has been subsidized by the taxpayer for years and now the tolls are so high that the tonnage has dropped dramatically. This Bill could have the same effect on the western farmer, and that is what I am nervous about. The Trans-Canada highway is subsidized by the taxpayer so that people can go on holidays. Economics are far more important than putting in a Trans-Canada highway. Highways should be the responsibility of the Provinces which have been collecting gas taxes for years for that purpose. Now the federal Government has to stick its nose in and subsidize the highways.
Another classic case of subsidization is Canadair, a transportation company which cost us $1,400 million. Now we find that de Havilland is going to cost $266 million.
The Government is asking farmers to give up their rights and is removing opportunity for producers and processors in the West. We must realize that this country is 5,000 miles long and 100 miles wide, and a little wider in the West. In Ontario, however, there is not much agriculture beyond 50 to 100 miles from the border.
We are committed to subsidizing transportation for grains and agricultural products. Every country in the world subsidizes agricultural products and transportation. We have a more serious problem than any other country, however, because our agricultural belt is so far from ocean ports. Now the Government is asking that we not allow farmers to have the freedom to choose what they want to do.
The subsidy in the United States amounts to between 30 per cent and 33 per cent and is paid directly to the farmer, not to the railway. He ships by rail and receives that amount of money back. France is another good example. At the end of World War II it was not self-sufficient in the production of grain but now it has become not only self-sufficient but is a net exporter of grain. The French Government gives farmers a 50 per cent subsidy on any grain shipped out of the country. That is the kind of arrangement we should have.
1 am not arguing that the railways do not need more funds, but those funds should flow from the farmers to the railways. If it happened that another form of transportation was more logical for some people than the Canadian National Railways, they should be permitted to use it. We are locking them in to the railways.
Western Grain Transportation Act
The point I am trying to make, Mr. Speaker, is that this is not right.
You are doing a poor job of it.

A subsidy to the railway is no guarantee that the railway will be improved. Railways are greedy and always have been. A recent example of that is that the CNR is now releasing a large number of employees because of new technology, compared to General Motors in my riding which is retraining every single employee so that they will not lose their jobs. This is a national disgrace, Mr. Speaker. That is the kind of thing that we should be speaking up for. I do not have faith in Crown corporations or in the railways. We must provide security, Mr. Speaker, for some processing of the grain in the West. It is far more economical to process the grain there, feed the beef and ship the beef out of the West. I know that some farmers in Ontario will not like that statement. However, I would like just briefly to explain that in Ontario they are fortunate. They are self-sufficient in grain. They are selfsufficient agriculturally, whereas the West, because it does not have the population, it does not have the same opportunity as those people in Ontario. However, I do stand on the principle of freedom of choice and I hope that this House will vote for this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to stand and speak in favour of the amendment to have a six-month hoist on this Bill. I would like to speak particularly from the point of view of the people of British Columbia who perhaps have not been quite as close to this issue and may not understand what great relevance it really has to them, both as Canadians and as British Columbians. "Keep the Crow", the clarion cry of western Canadians sometimes mystifies the people in British Columbia. "Why is this so important to farmers on the Prairies? Why is it so important that they will fight to retain the Crow freight rates, it seems, forever?"-and certainly I can say that from the point of view of Hon. Members of this caucus. "Why have thousands of people signed hundreds of petitions?", which incidentally the Government has restricted Members of Parliament in this Party from presenting, "And why are they so up in arms right across Canada and supported by people in all Provinces? Is the Crow rate important only to prairie farmers?"
I was very interested, Mr. Speaker, to learn that indeed the farmers of British Columbia will be equally affected by the removal of the Crow freight rate promises. In my research I learned that the incomes of British Columbia farmers would be cut by 30 per cent by 1992 as a result of this legislation. The cost of feed grains alone in British Columbia would be increased by 10 per cent because the feed grains come to B.C. from the prairie Provinces. It is a very important issue not only to farmers in B.C. but also it will have an impact on other workers in B.C. along with the rest of western Canada.

June 16, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
There are some superficial opinions which some people may have about this subject and I believe there is one Hon. Member among the Hon. Members who are so vocal across the way whom 1 would perhaps include in that group. I received a letter the other day from a person who asked, "By supporting Bill C-155, are you actually opposing job creation? Does it mean that you are against transportation improvements?" Categorically-and I hope the Hon. Member who is so lippy across the way will listen to this-we, of course, do not agree with this, and I will document that in a few moments. I would like to go, first of all, Mr. Speaker, to the basic Confederation agreement which was made regarding the Crowsnest freight rate. Mr. Allen Engel, the agriculture critic from Saskatchewan spoke in April to Members of Parliament of all Parties. He said the following:
-the Crow Rate is part of the ongoing Confederation bargain. It is an offset to higher costs borne by the West from such things as tariffs, the monopoly power of the railways, and the tremendous benefits given to the railways by the people of Canada since 1867.
You can't change this balance by only altering one component, ... If more money is needed to modernize the rail system, let everyone in Canada pay for that-not just western farmers.
Everyone in Canada, after all, will benefit from the trade dollars generated by the growing volumes of exports of various commodities produced in western Canada.
And if the Canadian public is going to invest in the rail system, it should get equity in return for that investment.
No more giveaways to the railways.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), as you are aware, Mr. Speaker, is a long time expert on the Crow rate and on transportation matters, generally. I would just like to refer quickly to comments he made, very eloquently, I believe, on "The Nation's Business". He said the following:
Back in the late 1800s the Canadian Pacific Railway received substantial mineral rights, land and cash from the people of Canada, in exchange for certain responsibilities. One of the obligations was to haul grain at the low Crow rate.
The Crowsnest Pass grain rate is the foundation of the western Provinces' union with the rest of Canada. Just as tariffs helped central Canada develop its industry, the Crow rate still helps western Canada get its grain over long distances to market.
Times change of course, but the geographical barrier separating our grain from market remains. Other countries grow their grain close to the cheap water transport or subsidize their grain transport. Without the Crow rate, our farmers today cannot easily afford to sell grain in competition with other countries.
He went on to explain, Mr. Speaker, that if the Crow goes, shipping subsidies in Atlantic Canada will be next. It is the same principle and is the same Liberal policy. Farmers who will lose 35 per cent of their incomes, of course will buy fewer supplies from central Canada, those tractors and farm implements, and much of the equipment which supply manufacturing jobs in central Canada. They will export less grain from British Columbia ports. The New Democratic Party estimates that by abandoning the Crow rate, it could cost 50,000 Canadians their jobs.
1 would like to point out to the average homemaker in British Columbia that the cost of bread in British Columbia will go up by at least five cents a loaf directly related to changing costs. If the Government removes the Crow rate subsidy, as it intends to do, cheaper transportation rates
through the United States will force farmers to export grain through the United States via CPR in the U.S., instead of through the ports of Canada. I was very interested in the information provided, again by our transport critic, that the CPR is already planning for this diversion of grain transportation through the United States. It has already taken advantage of the changes which are being proposed to expand its rails in the United States at a cost which would be less than using the St. Lawrence Seaway. On May 24, the same Hon. Member said that the CNR is showing evidence of doing the same thing. These railways should improve their tracks in Canada, not bail out the bankrupt Milwaukee Railroad in the United States where some $300 million was being used, which should have been used, of course, in Canada.
I would like to point out also, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill will have an immediate effect on my riding of Vancouver East. A lot of people in my constituency perhaps are quite unaware of this. If this grain and coal as well is diverted through the United States rather than coming west through the Rockies and into the Port of Vancouver, it will have a serious impact with loss of jobs for grain workers, longshoremen, and railway workers in Vancouver east and in the B.C. lower mainland, as well as people in businesses who service the port. There are alternative plans which, indeed, we have proposed to the Government. The Government proposes to make western farmers pay for an improved transportation system. We feel that everyone in Canada should pay for this, not just the farmers. Of course, we must modernize rail transportation as well as shipping facilities in western Canada, but we believe that the geography of Canada requires that everyone, not just farmers, pay for this.
Certainly we could go on forever about the deals the CPR has pulled over the years, including the real estate deals some of us question.
We in the New Democratic Party insist that the Crow rate was an agreement of Confederation and must be maintained as a national commitment, assisting everyone in Canada. We strongly support and urge the improvement of the transportation system to serve all parts of Canada. We need improved rails, new tunnelling, a boxcar industry, and we need that in British Columbia once again as well as port improvements. These are essential to Canada's economic recovery and the creation of jobs.
Money should be invested in improved transportation. We have advocated that $550 million a year be invested, but again with equity return so that Canadians will have control. We are also concerned about the coal agreements.

speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt the Hon. Member but the time allotted to her has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Crow rate reforms are just another shabby example of the Liberal Party's dedication to the philosophy that the end justifies the means. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his Cabinet know
June 16, 1983

exactly where the badly needed votes will be coming from in the next federal election and they will do anything in their power to make sure those votes are assured, even if that means creating disunity in a country that all of us in this Chamber love-well, most of us anyway. They will do that even if it means permitting drastic weaknesses in our agricultural economy.
Yes, we are aware that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has to some degree anyway studied the question of the Crow rate. We do not question his dedication to what is a very involved problem. We are aware that the Crow rate, as it now stands, is not without its imperfections. It is true that the rate of 1897 is not applicable to today's world. Yet the Minister's so-called solution really just creates another problem. The headaches caused by this proposal, if passed in its present form, will make past problems seem minimal by comparison. Nowhere in the new proposals can there be seen the slightest application of common sense or a sense of justice. Any notion of responsibility to the country as a whole I believe, is nonexistent.
The Minister has shown himself to be agreeable to the wishes of an alliance of self-interested individuals and pressure groups. I would hope that he would now have the good sense to pay close attention to those who have the courtesy to point out to him that the present course of action is indeed sheer and utter folly. I wonder if the Minister realizes that the repercussions of this decision will be drastic and also long lasting? Is he aware that this could cause the secondary agricultural industry in the West, particularly in Alberta, to die?
1 speak not as a westerner but as an eastern Canadian and an Ontarian who values the place of the western Provinces in Confederation and who deplores any action which tends to give them second billing. After all, where are the great wheat producing areas of our country? Where do we in the East obtain the materials which give us the prosperity we now enjoy? We all know. Indeed, the Minister knows. Yet he is about to cause an upheaval in our country which can only add to the great feeling of alienation shared by many and perhaps most westerners today.
As Dr. Gilson pointed out in his report, the distortion resulting from the Crow hampers all agricultural sectors in the Prairies, creating problems which are growing worse with inflation every day. The Crow is indeed a disincentive to railway investment, and the grain producer can no longer be assured of an adequate and responsive system to move his harvest.
I think the objective should then be to deal with the distortions and provide incentives to the railroads. It is hard to disagree that the freight rates must effectively be raised but the way to do it is certainly not to provide such huge subsidies to the railroads and then nothing to the farmers. The record of farmers is good. They have done more for the reputation of this country than any single group in Canada's history. Our bargaining power with the Soviet Union and China is a direct result of our massive grain exports to those countries.
Western Grain Transportation Act
Let us look at the reputation of the railways, Mr. Speaker. The name of the game has been branchline abandonment. Passenger service across this country is fast becoming a joke. Lines that were paying for themselves, for example the Atlantic run, just recently let go, and the Barrie to Toronto runs, have been cut back or dropped entirely. Meanwhile, mismanagement and overpayment of high officials are the real cause of the heavy losses incurred by the railways. Yet look who is receiving the subsidy.
Let us discuss further the potential for job losses. It is interesting to note the conflict between the Crow rate proposal and the special recovery program outlined in last month's sneaky-leaky budget. That program was designed to save jobs and the Crow rate proposal is guaranteed to destroy them. Thousands of jobs in the feeding, meat packing and food processing industries are going to be lost in the western part of our country.
Is it any wonder, then, that our Party is upset? That is where a great deal of our representation is from. We represent the western people and therefore we are truly the only national Party in this country. The Liberals have no stake in that part of the country, yet it reflects badly on them that they have chosen to ride roughshod over the best interests of that very important area.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that a powerful Quebec lobby is looking to its own best interests, realizing that the original Crow revision will have inevitably led to more agricultural diversification in the West. The areas of livestock processing and marketing of products are not the exclusive property of Quebec entrepreneurs. Is it just that they should have a monopoly on this? Is it fair that the West remain the raw material provider for the rest of the country instead of enjoying its own industry and the accompanying benefits? My answer is, I think not.
In some ways I very much admire the Minister of Transport. He has made an effort to persuade powerful Quebec Cabinet Ministers and the 74 Liberal MPs from la belle province to show some national spirit and some respect for the legitimate aspirations of the western Provinces and accept the proposals he outlined. Yet, selfishly, without long-term thought, they brought intense pressure upon the Minister to produce a half-baked compromise which brings out all the worst parts of the Bill and replaces the good ones.
The straight subsidy to the railroads, by far the most significant change in the proposal, can only add to the tragic list of plant closings in the meat processing industry in the West. Meanwhile the Quebec industry will profit. Pork producers, subsidized at great cost to the taxpayers, are living high off the hog in Quebec. Alberta now plays second fiddle to Quebec in that department. Is it really fair then, Mr. Speaker, that grain grown in Prairie fields can be bought as cheaply in Quebec as in Alberta? The Quebec producer does not have the same shipping costs as the Prairie beef man. However, he can have his livestock to market the same day with little or no weight loss. The Prairie beef producer ships his cattle East,

June 16, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
which takes days, at considerable cost in shrinkage and shipping. No wonder farmers are going bankrupt today.
Do the huge subsidies to the railroads guarantee that branchlines will not be abandoned and that good service at reasonable rates will be provided? I heard someone in the House say that the Minister has heart, and someone else said he is heartless. Maybe he has a carburetor instead of a heart, I am not sure, but he certainly should take another look at this Bill. I tend to doubt the Minister because of the past record of mismanagement. Listen to the tales of overnight closure of branchlines with the resultant death of full towns in the West. The trouble with a subsidy is that companies get used to them. They feel the word "efficiency" is no longer in the dictionary. They can go ahead and do whatever they please with the full knowledge that they will be bailed out when it is necessary.
Is my time running out? I have only three or four more sentences, Mr. Speaker; about 30 seconds.
In conclusion, I want to keep in mind the best interests of all Canadians. There can be no favouritism here. We are facing a major question of national unity. Regional differences are one matter, but political issues are at stake. Frankly, I think the proposal reeks of political engineering. In the long run, the future of our country is at stake.
I thank Your Honour for the extension of time.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin my short speech today by posing a question. Why is this major initiative to deal with the biggest transportation problem in the country today not worth careful and lengthy consideration by Parliament? Why is there this rush, this attempt to impose closure? Why is there such a decision by the Government, which it forces through because it has a majority, that the hours the House sits shall be extended to 11 o'clock in the evening three nights a week?
The proposed change in the Crow rate contained in the Bill at the present time, represents an attempt by the Government to impose an historic change on a region of Canada, western Canada, in which the Government has no members. I suggest that with a polarized Parliament such as this, in which the Liberal Government has no Members from the area where the legislation with which we are dealing will have such a major effect, it will change the established rights of that part of the country in a way and to an extent we have never seen before. I suggest that when those kind of changes are being brought forward, a Government which cares, one which wants to keep the country together, should have moved cautiously in wiping out the Crow rate, regarded by so many people in western Canada as being their Magna Carta.
People in western Canada and in Atlantic Canada have felt for many years that they are second class citizens, that their interests are sacrificed for the benefits of central Canada, for the benefits of Ontario and Quebec. The kind of provisions
contained in this Bill will go a long way toward convincing many people in western Canada that their fear is justified.
It has been argued by the President of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in support of the Government's plan, that it would put almost $1 billion into industrial, transportation and agricultural developments all across Canada. That is true. However, one must ask where that money will come from.
If one asks that question, one finds the answer to be very clear. The money would come from the pockets of Canadian farmers. Where would they obtain that money? They could not increase the price of the grain they sell, because if they did they could not compete with the Australians, the Americans or the Agentinians, all of whom are in very stiff competition with the Canadian farmer for their share of the world's grain market. Therefore, the Canadian grain farmer or producer would find his income reduced by the amount of the increase in the cost of transportation.
What would the Canadian farmer do? He would have to reduce the money he now spends and has spent for farm equipment, automobiles, trucks and other consumer goods. That would have an immediate effect on the farm equipment manufacturers and on the automobile companies, because they would use less steel, less rubber and less of all the products which go into producing the very heavy equipment they sell, and of which the farmer is a major, if not the major, purchaser.
The plan is supposedly to pump $16 billion into upgrading the transportation system. The farmer is told that it would only cost him 2 cents a bushel in the way of an increase. We know and the farmers know that that is just a beginning, that in fact, the increase will rise every year so that he will be looking at an increase in transportation costs over the next eight or ten years of something in the neighbourhood of 400 or 500 per cent.
There are people who are scandalized by the idea that a freight rate established in the 1890s should still be applied in the 1980s. Those people should remember several things. They should remember the principle of taxation, which is that any old tax is a fair tax, and any new tax is an unfair tax. It is true that 90 years have elapsed since the Crow rate went into effect, but all Governments since that time have had opportunities, which they have used, to review the Crow rate legislation and to change it. It has been scrutinized and examined by three or more Royal Commissions. All of them recommended against any change.
I am not opposed to a change in the Crow rate agreement under certain conditions. What are the conditions as I see them? The Crow rate was part of a package agreement. The railways agreed to move grain at a very cheap rate. They received compensation, the compensation being millions of dollars in cash grants, which they are still receiving, and millions of acres of land, some of the most valuable acreage in Canada. The Cominco property in Trail, B.C., was part of the land which the CPR received. Therefore, if the Government or anyone else wants to renegotiate the Crow agreement, I say let us renegotiate the whole agreement. We will ask the farmers
June 16, 1983

to give up the cheap rate for moving grain if and when the CPR gives back the money and the land which it received as part of the package.
Hear, hear!

That would be a fair deal and one to which I, and I think all Members of our Party, could agree.
The Canadian Pacific is one of the largest, if not the largest, corporation in this country. How did it get that way? It was as a result of the initial cash grabs and the land and other concessions it received. It would take me more time than that allotted to me just to list all the companies which the CPR owns-
As a result of what we gave them.

-as a result, of course, of what we gave them and upon which they built. I looked in the Financial Post's report on companies and found that CP Limited, in 1981-I will not list all the companies-had total assets of $16 billion. As far as I can tell, that does not include Cominco, of which it is a major shareholder, which had assets of more than $1 billion. It received that as a result of the deal it made back in 1890. We ought to keep that in mind when we speak of giving the hundreds of millions of dollars which this revision of the Crow rate will provide.
We in our Party are not opposed to modernizing and upgrading the railway system. How could I be opposed to that when I represent so many railway workers? Both the CNR and CPR in my city have recently had closures lasting for two and three months at a time. They have put thousands of workers who have worked for the company for up to 30 years on lay-off, for the first time in their history.
I have told the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) that this is idiotic. We know that our shipments of grain, sulphur, coal and potash will increase greatly in ten years. I have been telling the Government for the last couple of years that now is the time to modernize the system. We are not opposed to modernizing the system. We want the railways to get on with the job of upgrading their system in order to move all of our goods.
However, we do not want this to be done at the expense of the farmers or at the expense of the railway workers. We say that the farmers should not be required to shoulder the capital burden, as we believe this Bill will force them to do, that will be required to move the coal, sulphur, potash and other bulk commodities. We say that this Bill does not accomplish that, and we are opposed to it for that reason.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join my colleagues in today's ongoing debate on Bill C-155, the Western Grain Transportation Act, or the Crow
Western Grain Transportation Act
rate as it is commonly called, because of its unquestioned importance to all Canadians. Although I usually only participate in debates relating to the scientific and industrial development of our great country, I feel I should make my views known on this important Bill because, as all Members know, it does not affect only one particular part of Canada, namely the western region, but every other part of Canada as well.
The controversy over the Crow rate has resulted in a national debate on the topic, as it well should. The Crow rate is a special rail freight rate that is applied to the transportation of export grain and stems from an agreement between the federal Government and the Canadian Pacific Railway back in September of 1897. As part of the agreement, the CPR agreed to maintain the Crow rate in perpetuity in return for land and federal aid in building the railway in the mineral-rich Kootenay region of southern British Columbia.
A short while ago I had the opportunity to briefly discuss this Bill with a number of my constituents at a brunch in my riding. One of my constituents stated that he felt the Crow rate was, in his words, a western problem and that as a resident of Ontario he did not feel he had very much at stake in this issue.
Regrettably, my constituent was wrong. It has been demonstrated decade after decade, in country after country that a healthy agricultural community is the basis for a healthy and strong economy of a country as a whole. This is particularly true in Canada's case where we depend on billions of foreign dollars to come to Canada to pay for the wheat and other grains we export.
As transportation costs are a big item in any farmer's budget, and because the Government of 1897, unlike the present Government, wanted to protect this important industry, the Crow rate was imposed upon the railroads to ensure that distance would not be a fatal charge for the wheat growers. In return for the special rate imposed on the railroads for the benefit of farmers the railroads were given vast grants of land and other concessions in perpetuity for the benefit of the railroad.
There is not a farmer anywhere in the West in any community who will argue that the rate set so many years ago should apply in the same terms today. They will admit that times have changed. But the solution put forward by the Government to give the benefits to the railroads with no concessions at all to the western farmers is completely unacceptable.
Can anyone seriously argue that the railroads are being victimized by a fixed freight rate which is far below today's actual cost of grain transportation, while ignoring the huge gain in the asset value of the lands and concessions given to the railways when they entered into the agreement? If one argues that the lands cannot be taken back for today's value without destroying the railroads-unlike my friends to my left who somehow believe that the lands could be given back, destroying the railroads totally, to all of our disadvantage-then why should we not be as concerned about the other party to the agreement, the grain farmer who similarly could be destroyed? Perhaps we should consider giving proportionate shares in the

June 16, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
railroad to the farmers in return for increased freight rates. At least in that manner they would benefit from this one-sided solution to the problem.
Whatever solutions may lie ahead, it should not be to the detriment of one key segment of our society which year after year and at great personal financial risk grows and exports a renewable Canadian resource to the benefit of us all. While the Government may have nothing to lose in western Canada politically, the country has a great deal to lose if the Government continues to ignore what is a legitimate regional concern of the country, or how this Bill will affect the other regions of Canada.
If anything has resulted thus far in the debate, it has been a demonstration of the failure of the Government to understand Canada and those forces which bring it together and make it work. It has shown its failure to understand the differences so it can ultimately reconcile them.
Bill C-155 has widened the consensus gap. The country has moved further away from consensus on changing the Crow rate even since the announcement by the Minister of Transport to modify the Bill. Whatever general feeling or consensus existed in the West has disappeared. Not only are the grain farmers and the livestock producers bitter and angry, the modification to the Bill to make all payments to the railways has not entirely satisfied the pools. The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool is still asking for more changes.
Let us look for a moment at this piece of complex legislation which bears the Liberal trademark of complexity and bureaucracy. Let us examine why the statutory Crow rate is so important to western Canada.
The statutory rate is a constitutional pillar which provides stability, simplicity and certainty to western Canadian grain producers. At .05 cents a tonne mile, the rate has been a valuable tool for producers in their planning. The statutory rate is about the only farm input cost providing cost certainty to farmers. The statutory rate provided the historical, social and economic base of western Canada which was founded on the production, distribution and marketing of grain. The statutory rate was a trade off and acted as a counterbalance protection from industrial based central Canada. The statutory rate recognized that Canada, as a trading nation, must be competitive and it buffered farmers from the artificial and natural advantages of other grain exporting countries. The statutory rate recognized that grain and oil seeds were natural assets to Canada, contributing positively to the balance of trade and economic spin-offs.
There are a number of ways in which this Liberal Government has betrayed the statutory rate and Members should know why our Party opposes the existing Bill. First, the principles of the statutory freight rate are not retained in this legislation. There is no guarantee of international competitiveness for the future.
Second, the freight rate structure will provide for openended escalation without consideration for farmers' profit positions or
the value of grain. The National Energy Program has escalated the cost of gasoline and diesel for farm equipment and has also driven up the other major cost factor, agricultural chemical fertilizers, to the point where a bushel of Canadian wheat costs over $1 more than in the United States. This latest Government bungle will further hurt the western farmer.
Third, the 31.1 million tonne cap will provide a disincentive to increase grain production. That is amazing. Any company sales manager knows enough to increase a salesman's incentive by offering greater reward for increased volume. Only a bungling bureaucrat could come up with a system that penalizes a farmer for producing more wheat and revenue for Canada.
Fourth, the blended freight rate and the prospect of variable rates will create a further disincentive.
Fifth, the Bill is a costly mechanism which will pay bureaucrats to produce more paperwork rather than farmers to produce wheat.
Sixth, the Bill will further mitigate against diversification and processing of agricultural production in western Canada.
Seventh, the Bill is overly generous to railways while neglecting the alternative means of shipping, such as commercial trucking or the farmers' own trucks.
Eighth, no provision has been made to reduce rates if costs should fall.
Finally, there are inadequate rail service performance guarantees and no incentive for the grain transport system to be cost effective and efficient.
We in this Party are not without positive suggestion and ideas with respect to this Bill and we have made them. The Government of Canada and the railways have a continuing obligation to provide a special low rate to assist Canadian producers competing with subsidized grain export nations or this valuable export of renewable resources will decline.
As well, producers should be guaranteed an efficient, cost effective and reliable grain transportation system. Producers should have the option, or choice, to ship their grain in the most cost effective way, whether by truck or train, rather than in certain instances being locked into inefficient local grain storage elevators and poorly serviced branch rail lines which, in many cases, simply adds to the cost of the product, reduces the farmers' profits, does nothing for the railway and serves the country badly. I believe I have one minute left, Mr. Speaker.

Grain producers must have a statutory freight rate which preserves the benefits of the Crow and must be protected from open-ended escalation.
We are dealing with what is probably one of the most important pieces of legislation to be brought before the House

in this session. This Government must not continue to act in its usual cavalier way but stop, look, and listen to what responsible and knowledgeable people are saying is wrong and damaging about this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to speak in support of the amendment of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), that Bill C-155 be given a six-month hoist. I do so because the Bill is a confusing piece of legislation. It incorporates three different principles, and we should not have to deal with them all at the same time. It is not good legislation.
Simultaneously, the Government has done a good job to persuade some people that this legislation will benefit them. In British Columbia particularly there are some sectors of society and the economy that feel this amendment to the Crow legislation will be beneficial. Most of us who are Members from British Columbia have received telegrams from major forest industries urging quick passage of the Bill. I note that on June 10 the Hon. Minister of Transportation and Highways for British Columbia spoke before a ports convention. I shall read some of his comments:
We also recognize the importance of passing the legislation before Parliament rises at the end of this month. The changes that are proposed by the federal Government are critical to western Canada, its industry, its transportation system, and its communities. Like our national ports, the railways need a commercial base and a commitment of financial resources that will allow them to put the capacity in place that will be needed to move our resource products to world markets. There will be no point in developing our ports to handle growth if development plans are not matched by the railways.
Unfortunately, for the people of British Columbia, the Minister of Transportation and Highways, Mr. Fraser, sees only one aspect of the change. He isolates one factor and then uses it to suggest that the entire package will be beneficial to the people of British Columbia. That is just not the case because it ignores two basic things. First, by doing away with the statutory rates on grain shipments and allowing increased costs for shipping grain it opens the door for the possible diversion of grain to American ports in the Louisiana Gulf states because of higher Canadian freight rates. We have to ask what effect this will have on major British Columbia ports such as Prince Rupert, and especially Vancouver.
It has already been pointed out today that both the CN and the CP are involved in trying to gain control of old railways in the United States. We have to ask what is the purpose of that if it is not to serve as a way of funnelling Canadian goods through the United States? What is the purpose of us having American lines in the midwest? I suggest it is for export.
The second factor is especially important to British Columbia. It involves the Dominion coal lands. On March 15 my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker), raised his concern and the concern of all Members of this Party about the 50,000 acres of Dominion coal
Western Grain Transportation Act
lands, worth some $450 billion, which were turned over to the Dominion Government as part of the original Crowsnest agreement. Clause 62 of the Bill leaves these lands with the federal Government. If this agreement is ended, why are these lands not to be returned to British Columbia so that the people of B.C. can begin to enjoy their benefit?
These lands are the richest coal lands we have in the Province at the present time, yet this Bill leaves them entirely at the mercy of an order in cabinet so the CPR or some corporation can get them again. The people of B.C. are not getting them again. That is why I and other Members of my Party would urge the Government of British Columbia to take a closer look at this Bill, and realize it is not totally favourable to the people of B.C.
It is not just wheat, but the total economy of our country that is involved. Other speakers in our Party from Ontario have pointed out the detrimental effects this Bill can have on the farm machinery implement sector of their economies. Of course, in our Party we are not only concerned about British Columbia, Ontario and the Prairies, we are concerned about the totality of the nation. We see this as one nation. We see the injury to one part of the nation as an injury to the entire nation.
In that connection I would like to read a short passage from "The Rowell Sirois Report" as follows:
Without the construction of all-Canadian transportation facilities and an appropriate structure of freight rates (and the huge public assistance which that entailed) each of the regions would have linked up with the railway system of the United States. The connections between the various parts of the country would then have been made through the economically and politically aggressive neighbour to the south. This development would have been much less costly; it would have avoided the vast overhead of bridging great physical barriers, and it would have enabled the most intensive use of facilities already available. With the lower costs which this would have permitted, the export industries would have expanded further, the rise in the value of their natural resources would have been greater and the income obtained would have been larger. There would, however, have been no secure economic basis for a Canadian nation. Hence purely economic criteria were put aside for the creation and maintenance of a political entity.
I suggest those comments are as true today as they were in the 1930s when they were written. An injury to one part of the nation is an injury to all. If we open up the way for the diversion of Canadian grain to American ports, we will be harming British Columbia. If we reduce the cash income of prairie farmers we will be doing damage to the manufacturers in Ontario.
Certainly people in our Party have documented the negative effect these changes will have on Canadian farmers. There will be a 500 per cent increase in the cost of moving grain between now and 1991. This will force small and medium-sized farmers off the land. We have seen the results in my Province of federal government policies and the way they have forced small and medium-sized fishermen out of their jobs. Now we see the same kind of thing being applied to farmers.
We are concerned about the effects of these changes on small communities. With variable freight rates there will be

much more use made of large trucks, branch lines, and branch elevators will be closed. Communities are going to be killed.

Mr. Speaker, an article appearing in the April 15 edition of the Vancouver Sun criticized British Columbia Members of Parliament for not presenting the Province's case for changes in the Crows-nest freight rate structure. The person responsible for making this assertion was no less than Mr. Don Lanskail, President and Chief Executive Officer of the Council of Forest Industries of British Columbia, commonly referred to as COFI. In the article, Mr. Lanskail is referred to as one of B.C.'s best-known lobbyists. His ties to the federal Liberal Party are well known and his Liberal credentials are impeccable. Not long ago he was rewarded by an appointment to the Board of Directors of the Canada Post Corporation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Some reward!

I remember hearing someone recount the events that took place when Mr. Lanskail, this good lobbyist, attended his first Canada Post Corporation board meeting in Ottawa. Evidently he was picked up at his Vancouver office by a limousine, handed a first-class return ticket to Ottawa, picked up at the Ottawa airport by a limousine and installed in a suite in the Chateau Laurier. When it came time to return to Vancouver, the same procedure held in reverse. Limousines and suites for the high-rollers; taxis, buses and rooms are for the great unwashed. No wonder it costs more to mail a letter than to ship a bushel of export grain.
On May 9 of this year I received my first communication from Mr. Lanskail in his position as president of COFI, urging me to support the Minister and his Crow legislation. Along with his letter was a document entitled "The Position of the
Council of Forest Industries of B.C. regarding rail transportation capacity and statutory rates" dated August 1981. This was from the man who said in April of this year that British Columbia M.P.'s were remiss, if not late, in representing our Province on the Crow issue. Rather strange indeed that he saw fit to sit on a position paper for almost two years before it occurred to him that perhaps it should be shown to someone other than his Liberal friends in Ottawa. Perhaps he is overrated as one of B.C.'s best lobbyists.
In his letter, Mr. Lanskail proposes that we fully support the Minister's proposal, and also that we are expected to support the 1981 COFI position. If he had taken the time to re-read the 1981 paper he had hidden away, and to check it against the Minister's legislation, he surely would have noticed that the two are in serious conflict. For example, point four on page 13 of the COFI documents states, "Government funding should preferably be paid to the producers if a subsidy is required". They are advocating that Government funding should preferably be paid to the producers. Come, come, Mr. Lanskail, what are we to do? In your headlong rush to fall into line as a good Liberal, you have failed to amend your own position of 1981.
The other thing that annoyed B.C. Members of Parliament, and this was previously raised in the House by the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) and the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), is the telex received on May 9 by all B.C. Members from Mr. Ken Benson, President and CEO of B.C. Forest Products Limited. He also urges us to forget our responsibilities to the rest of Canada and to support the Government line. Being aware of the B.C. resource industries' situation, we can understand their position, and I will refer to this later.
However, what we could not tolerate was the fact that Mr. Benson had been clumsy enough to send his telex for distribution to the Prime Ministers office. This practice may be economical and efficient, but it may have been more effective if we had been approached via the same avenues available to most Canadians. Being lobbied courtesy the Prime Minister's Office does not sit well with B.C. Members. I suggest Mr. Benson and Mr. Lanskail have something to learn about lobbying B.C. Members of Parliament. Fortunately, many executives of the B.C. forest industry are not connected to the Liberal Party and to those good people who we have listened to well and attentively.
Let us now look at some facts about the Crow rate and British Columbia. The main argument for altering the Crow rate centres around the fact that there is little incentive for railways to improve their western systems. In particular, the forest and mining industries are concerned that capacity constraints will cause a bottleneck for the shipment of their products. This is a factor of increasing urgency, not only to these industries but to Canada's export markets.
For example, in 1960 grain dominated the bulk exports through the mountains to the West coast. By the mid-1970s,
June 16, 1983

coal had surpassed grain by tonnage in these bulk exports. The latest agreements to sell B.C. metallurgical coal to Japan and other Pacific rim countries promises to continue this trend.
In 1979, forest products from B.C. made up 60 per cent of provincial exports and almost 9 per cent of Canadian exports. In 1982, a total of 4.94 billion board feet of B.C. lumber was shipped by rail. Of that total, 3.6 billion board feet was exported to the United States. Comparatively, shipment by water accounted for three billion board feet and highway shipment accounted for approximately 2.4 billion board feet. Obviously adequate rail service is vital to the good health of both the lumber and mining industries.
In 1981 the Council of Forest Industries of British Columbia argued that rationing of western rail services was imminent because current rail capacity was going to be unable to meet the demand. This possibility has been delayed by the recession which caused severe cutbacks in lumber production. However, the point remains that rail service in B.C. must be improved in order for the B.C. economy to expand in coming years.
This does not mean that British Columbia should adopt the Government's proposals as outlined in Bill C-155. Probably of greatest significance is the fact that the current legislation fails to provide adequate rail service performance guarantees. Furthermore, there is no incentive for the grain transport system to be cost effective and efficient.
There is no doubt that this Bill is generous to the railways. Under this Bill the railways will receive 100 per cent of their long-run variable costs, 20 per cent contributions to overhead and 20.5 per cent contributions to capital. In fact, by 1990 the railways will receive a 100 per cent increase in the freight rate as compared to today. Mr. Carl Snavely, who has been commissioned by the Government on numerous occasions to determine the cost of moving grain, has stated that these provisions are too generous. Unfortunately, the Government has failed to ensure that money provided to the railroads will in fact be used to increase service at a rate required to increase and improve the system. Furthermore, for the forest and mineral sectors, there is an added disadvantage in that the British Columbia Railway will not benefit from such subsidies. Therefore, services provided by B.C. Rail will be slower to improve. Furthermore, there are no benefits to truckers in the proposed legislation.
All in all, the proposals outlined in Bill C-155 fail to provide the necessary measures to guarantee the improved service required by the B.C. resource industries which depend so heavily on the country's transportation system.
I would now like to briefly discuss how cattleman in British Columbia will be affected by changes in the Crow rate. At present, the Crow rate causes higher pricing for grain for feed in the West. The Crow artificially keeps transportation costs below what they will be without the price ceiling, so farmgate prices are higher in the west than they would be without the Crow. These higher prices reduce livestock production in the West.
Would the proposals of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) alleviate this problem? Not at all. In fact, according to
Western Grain Transportation Act
the Minister's own figures, these proposals will result in a loss of an additional $1 billion in livestock production and an additional $350 million worth of economic activity with respect to processing, packing plants and the feedmill industry in the West. This is not progress, Mr. Speaker.
The Progressive Conservative Party will propose an amendment which will make the Crow rate benefit optional. It will allow the producer the freedom to choose between methods of shipment and guarantee that railways will provide adequate service. We also propose that the railways should receive fair and adequate compensation in order to provide the necessary capital and maintenance of plant and equipment. We recognize that an increase in rail capacity is an absolute necessity and that railways will need extra funding to do this. However, this should not be at the expense of producers and adequate guarantees must be provided.
Finally, while I am a Member of Parliament from British Columbia, I am also a representative of all Canadians. It would be unthinkable for me to take any action which would be unfair to my fellow Canadians in other regions. Therefore, it is imperative that the Government ensure that prairie farmers retain the benefits of the Crow in order that they can compete with foreign producers who benefit from government subsidies. Failure to do so would be a disaster, not only to prairie farmers but also for the entire Canadian economy.
The proposals before the House today benefit neither the forest, mining nor cattle industries of British Columbia, nor do they provide a reasonable benefit sufficient for prairie grain farmers to remain competitive in the export market. For these reasons, the Government must adopt the amendments put forward by the Progressive Conservative Party when they come before the House.

Western Grain Transportation Act
Prince Rupert, Thunder Bay or Montreal, then the people who work on the rail line in communities like The Pas, Wabowden, Gillam and Churchill, and those who work at the Port of Churchill and live in those communities will suffer very, very much.

Mr. Speaker, when I first looked at the Bill I saw that it was a Bill for the movement of western grain. It should have been described as the railway subsidy Bill. It is a $651 million Bill to provide money for the railways. It does not require them to do a damn thing. They get $651 million per year for the next five years, then the situation is reviewed and we give them more money. They do not have to spend a nickle or a dime on track or improving transportation in Canada. This is a Bill to give $651 million to the railways.
If the Government were to present the Bill in that fashion, in that fashion only, and not tied to the movement of grain, then we might discuss the question of whether the Government of Canada should use the taxpayers' money to support the railways-but it proposes to tie it to the movement of grain. I say to you that there is nothing in the Bill that ties the subsidies to the railways and what the railways might do with that money for the movement of grain. The railways are not required to put down a single tie, lay a single length of track, or improve a single terminal. They are not required to do a darn thing but still, they get $651 million.
There may be some requirement in terms of moving grain and the products of the country but there is no requirement to improve the service or do anything other than they are doing already. It is a railway subsidy Bill.
My friend from the riding of Churchill spoke about the line owned by the Canadian National Railways which runs to the Port of Churchill. I have travelled that line by passenger train; it goes up and down through the muskeg; it carries freight cars provided they are not too loaded and provided the train is not too big or is not too heavy. You can get a train across that line although it is not much of a line. One begins to wonder why in 1983 we should have a railway line built to the standard and quality of that particular line. There is nothing in the Bill that requires the Government or the railways to use any of its $651 million to rebuild the line to the Port of Churchill. They do not have to rebuild that port either. There is absolutely nothing in the Bill. It subsidizes railways and does not do anything for the farmers or to improve the transportation of the country. The railways get money. Canadian Pacific may build up a bigger dividend and Canadian National may not have quite the loss it would normally have, but there is nothing in the Bill to require any improvement to rail transportation in the country.
Only certain parts of the grain growing areas of the prairie region are covered by the Bill. New land that may be opened up at some time and is not presently covered by the Crow rate subsidy is not included so it is only a portion of the grain growing area of western Canada that is included. It is not all protected by the Bill. This is a discriminatory Bill-a Bill that says Canada finished growing in 1982.
If you were to clear land in 1983 or 1984 and were to decide to grow grain, you would not be covered. The Bill is antiCanadian; it is against growth in Canada. This Bill is designed to terminate Canada. This Bill is a central Canadian Bill
Western Grain Transportation Act
formulated in Mount Royal where, as far as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is concerned, Canada has already grown to its maximum capacity.
The new lands in Canada cannot be developed because they will be subject to penalty. They will not receive any assistance in terms of transportation. If crop is grown on those new lands they will pay the full rate. Only the existing lands are to be covered. What kind of Bill to build Canada is this? It is a disaster Bill. It is a Bill that really does nothing to create the growth we need.
Let us look at some other parts of the Bill. This Party has suggested some sort of system whereby the Crow benefit-and there is no question that there is a Crow benefit because those who grow grain are directly or indirectly receiving a subsidy for the transportation of their crop to the seaport-should be paid directly to the farmer. Why should it not be? The farmer should use the money in the way he wants to-to hire the kind of transportation he wants to hire. If that transportation involves the hiring of a tractor and semi to haul grain to Vancouver or Thunder Bay, so be it. Perhaps he then transfers it to a port in the United States.
One thing about tractor-trailer transportation in Canada is that it can be a two-way street. At the moment there is more tractor-trailer transportation of commodities into western Canada than there is transportation of products out from western Canada. A great deal of capacity already exists on tractor-trailers out of western Canada that travel empty. The capacity is there to carry a great deal of our grain to port at compensatory rates. It is a pleasure this evening to rise to speak on the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). There is no doubt that this particular legislation has caused a great deal of consternation across the country. It is a proposal to abandon a very long tradition in this country, a tradition which has supported one of the major economic sectors of the Canadian economy, the agricultural sector, as well as others, and it should not be abandoned in the way the
present Government has decided. There is no doubt that there are a great many problems with our transportation system which have developed over the years. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that those problems in our transportation system are due in large part to the failure of the Government to fulfil its responsibilities and insist on investment by railways in upgrading the rail system in order to be provided with certain kinds of assistance over a period of time, and to insist that that rail system provide adequate transportation for goods and services in Canada.
The reason we are here today, Mr. Speaker, and I imagine it will be for a much longer period of time, is as a result of the tremendous controversy which exists in the country over this particular piece of legislation, this attempt to place on the backs of Canadians the responsibility which, in fact, should have been taken by the railway companies. I am referring both to the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian Pacific Railway was given enormous concessions in the Province of British Columbia and, indeed, across Canada. I would like to deal just briefly with my own Province of British Columbia in which from Victoria to Seymour Narrows, some one hundred odd miles up the coast of Vancouver Island, the Canadian Pacific Railway was given a 40-mile wide strip of land, forest and mineral resources, provided that it build a railroad to Victoria and that it continue to operate that railroad. The system contained enormous resources of coal, of timber and of land. Today we find companies like Marathon Realty with enormous land holdings which are based on that original grant given for the commitment the railway made to the people of Canada. The timber resources were used to catapult Canadian Pacific into large shareholding positions in major forest companies, including MacMillan Bloedel. Undoubtedly, the coal situation was exploited as well.
What we have today is a rail line going up and down Vancouver Island which is in very poor shape and it is proposed that it be abandoned. That is the Esquimalt-Nanaimo railroad. This particular piece of railroad is of intense interest to the people who live on Vancouver Island. It symbolizes the betrayal of Canadians by the railway companies. In a small section of this country, one strip of railroad runs just basically between Victoria and Courtney and is of tremendous interest to the people of Vancouver Island. The railway company has struggled for years to abandon that piece of territory. It has taken all the resources, taken away the benefits provided by the lands, the forests and the mineral resources. Now that they are gone, it does not want to operate the rail system any more. It does not want to keep the railroad upgraded and continually it has tried to abandon that entire system. Potentially it is probably one of the most lucrative trunks of the rail system in the country. With some input, some sincere input from the companies which now operate services on it, there is no doubt that a very viable transportation system on Vancouver Island could be developed. That is an example of areas where the railway has not become involved in developing its service,
June 16, 1983

especially in the marketing area. The railroad owners do not market properly the services of transportation. There are new ski resorts, new tourist facilities by the drove on Vancouver Island. There is a tremendous influx of people into the capital city of British Columbia, Victoria. Certainly, those kinds of opportunities to develop new markets have never been taken advantage of by the railway companies.
There is also a tremendously successful venture which has been put on to capitalize on tourism by the Government of British Columbia with the Royal Hudson railroad system in which the old steam locomotives were brought back and run on a tourist section over a period of time, bringing back history and enhancing tourism. This has been proposed numerous times for Vancouver Island, but the railway companies reject it out of hand. They want nothing to do with that stretch of railroad. They do not want to enhance the transportation of goods. They do not want to enhance tourism. In fact, they are into far more lucrative activities. They do not want to run the railroad any more. It costs too much money. The railway guaranteed to run that system in perpetuity. It guaranteed to build it. It has failed in its guarantee and we should take back the resources and take the railroad business out of there. It should become a public venture, a public utility.
The legislation which is before us today is reprehensible. It is the responsibility of the railways to build a railroad system, an effective railroad system in Canada, and those companies have failed to do so. The Canadian Pacific Railway is attempting to take money earned in Canada and buy 800 miles of railroad in the United States, to build and operate. It is absolutely contemptible that a company which is going to attempt to load the costs of building and maintaining a railroad system in Canada, for which it obtained billions of dollars in resources, is turning around and telling the Canadian farmer and Canadian taxpayer that they must build their railroad system if it is going to continue to operate it, and at the same time removing capital earned in this country to invest elsewhere. The CNR tried to acquire 2,100 miles of rail on the old Milwaukee line in the United States. A Crown corporation was taking capital from Canada instead of building and running the railroad system here. They want to abandon it and place the responsibility on the backs of taxpayers.
