Member for Bow River has narrated the story about arriving in the coal mining community of Drumheller, where i was born, in a wagon in 1915.1 do not want to date him but he can speak much better than I about how important it has been to have the benefit of the Crow rate in order to ensure that the promise of western Canada was realized by so many of us.
It was my own great grandfather, Mr. Speaker, who packed his family in a boxcar three springs in succession and moved into the foothills of Alberta to a place called Westward Ho and established a farm there. He had returned to Ontario each year because of the difficult conditions, but finally, because of a strong-minded wife and a desire to become a part of the West, they stayed and the family spread and many of my relatives went into farming in Alberta and Saskatchewan. I know just how important this Crow rate is and how important it is that we do not make any major alterations in this historic rate structure established in 1897 and confirmed by an Act of Parliament in 1925. It is so fundamental to the culture and underpinnings of western Canada.
I have recollections of hauling grain with my uncles to grain elevators. I drove my first vehicle sitting in my uncle's lap. It was a John Deere tractor. I remember putting posts in and working late at night in the Prairie dust where real men knew
what real hard work was about. It would not have been possible to develop western Canada and build the communities, schools, churches, highways and all that has materialized in the West had it not been for this very fundamental measure, the statutory rate for shipping from those very bountiful grain-producing areas in western Canada. It is important that we recognize all of those pioneers and many new Canadians who came with the turn of the century to cut trees, pull stumps and set up small sawmills and clear land. Those same people singing songs around the piano are really part and parcel of the culture of western Canada. They would not have realized the great benefits they have today had it not been for this historical Crow rate structure.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Vegreville, pointed out in this House a few weeks ago that farmers today are receiving $4.63 a bushel for wheat, and ten years ago they received $4.57. He pointed out just how little the price that is available to the western farmer has increased over the past ten years and how fragile is their situation, particularly in light of inflation in terms of fertilizer costs, land costs and interest costs, and the plight of the family farm which is susceptible to any major changes in the cost of shipping grain to port and to market.
Therefore, it is essential that the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. Benjamin) be supported in the House because, as I have pointed out, and as many of our colleagues have pointed out, this legislation and initiative, which has only been before the House for about five weeks, is so fundamental to the culture and to the future destiny of western Canadians that it cannot be passed through the House in the twinkling of an eye. We cannot allow the Government to run roughshod over the rights and aspirations of so many western Canadians.
If one reads the Bill and its provisions with respect to calculating the actual rate which farmers will pay, one finds that there will be an utter lack of predictability on the part of the western grain producer as to what his costs will be from year to year. It is a very complicated, bureaucratically designed formula which will make it impossible to determine. Faced with the fluctuations in world price structure for grains and other agricultural commodities, it will be virtually impossible for the western producer to have the security of being able to plan ahead to know what area should be planted, what amount of equipment he can count on purchasing, such as new tractors, combines and the like, because of the uncertainty which this sudden change will impose upon him.
I realize it is designed so that the increase in the rate for grain would be gradually phased in, and there is much talk of a healthy subsidy to the farmers, something like $650 million a year. But in fact this will not be a subsidy to the farmer; it will be a direct cash grant to the railways. It is the railways of western Canada that we thank for helping to bind together all those rural communities and, in my own Province of British
June 16, 1983

Columbia, the resource enterprises of the various saw mills, pulp mills and mining operations. Therefore, we are grateful to the contribution the railways have made to the development of western Canada, but we also realize that they have obtained considerable benefits in return for the services they have provided in building railways and communities and binding together the people of western Canada.
We now read that the federal Government, as one condition of this agreement, will completely disavow any prior commitments with respect to a major block of natural resource, and that is known as the Dominion coal block in the area of southeast British Columbia, in that this block of between one billion tonnes and 8.5 billion tonnes of first rate metallurgical coal will become a windfall to the federal Government if this legislation is allowed to proceed in its present form. In fact, that coal block was a gift from the Province of British Columbia in return for a guarantee that the railways would continue to modernize and operate their services throughout western Canada and to provide for the shipment of grain, timber, mineral products and everything else that is rolling on the rails. The federal Government will have realized a windfall of between $16 billion and $75 billion if the legislation goes through.
1 think it is time we studied many of these factors in much greater detail. I therefore heartily endorse the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Regina East. I hope we can get on with passing it so that we can have this legislation set aside for another six months.

I bring again to your attention the rule with regard to complicated questions. I point out to you that the application of the rule goes back to 1888, and I quote:
In 1888, ... the Speaker ruled that two propositions which were then before the House in one motion could be taken separately if any Member objected to their being taken together.
He goes on to say:
Although this ruling does not appear to have been based on any previous decision, it has since remained unchallenged.
The key is as follows:
A complicated question can, however, only be divided if each part is capable of standing on its own.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the question we now have before us, Bill C-155, is indeed a complicated question within the definition of Erskine May. I put it to you in the following way, Sir, for your consideration: There are three distinct principles contained within Bill C-155. Each of the distinct principles can be spelled out. Each one is capable of standing on its own merit. The principles are as follows: In the first section of the Bill, known as Part I, the Bill deals with administrative measures to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of grain. I submit that that is a question of principle, the decision on which should be made by the House of Commons separate and apart from the other parts of the Bill. The decision on the administrative measures to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of grain could be quite easily introduced in a Bill without either of the other two principles contained in this Bill being before the House of Commons. I will come back to that point in a moment.
The second principle contained within the Bill is the principle which speaks directly to the rates which will be established to be charged to farmers for the transportation of grain. I submit to you, Sir, that that is a principle quite different from the administrative measures to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of grain. The rates are a matter which could easily be dealt whith by the House of Commons in a separate Bill, as a separate principle.
The third principle in the Bill is the disposition of what is known as the Dominion coal lands. I put before the House, Mr. Speaker, that that principle alone, how the Dominion coal lands are disposed of and dealt with, is a principle which can stand on its own separate and apart from either of the other two.
1 raise the three principles because I want to suggest to you, Sir, that it is important for parliamentarians to be able to vote as their conscience dictates on each of the principles. I suggest to you that the principle which speaks to the redevelopment and administration of the railroads is a principle in its own right, not necessarily hinging on whether or not there is a change to the statutory grain rates or to the Dominion coal lands. The principle of changing the statutory grain rate is a
Western Grain Transportation Act
principle which can stand on its own merit and is not necessarily related to any redevelopment or upgrading of the railroad system, or to the disposition of the Dominion coal lands. I suggest to you, Sir, that the matter of the Dominion coal lands and its disposition is a principle separate and apart from the principle of the redevelopment of the rail transportation system and separate and apart from the imposition of any freight rate of any kind at all, grain or otherwise.
Therefore, we have three quite distinct questions before us and these are questions on which Hon. Members cannot necessarily vote en bloc. These are questions which deal with entirely different matters. There would be Hon. Members in the House of Commons who would want to vote one way or the other on how the Government of Canada should dispose of or deal with the Dominion coal lands. They would want to do that without any regard to whether or not we upgrade the railroad and without any regard to whether or not there are changes undertaken to the Crowsnest Pass arrangement as it applies to the freight rates charged to grain growers in western Canada. There are people in this House of Commons, men and women representing constituencies from all across Canada, who would want to be able to vote on the principle contained in the section which speaks to the redevelopment of Canada's railroad system, separate and apart from the question of whether or not there is a disposition of the Dominion coal lands, and separate and apart from whether or not there is a change which takes place to the grain freight rates as contained in the third principle. There are again Hon. Members who would want to vote one way or the other on the grain freight rates changes which are being proposed.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is ample evidence to show that Parliaments have in fact on a number of occasions dealt with complicated questions such as this by requiring that the question be split for the purpose of the vote, that the question be split into the three principal parts in order that each Hon. Member be able to exercise his or her responsibility in the way which he or she sees fit as they understand it, given that their constituencies may well have quite different needs and quite different priorities. The way this Bill is structured makes it impossible. It is necessary for an Hon. Member to vote on all three principles at one time whether or not that Hon. Member believes that the same vote is capable of reflecting his honest opinion as to how each of the three principles should be dealt with.
I would like to urge upon you that you give serious consideration to the implications of allowing a Bill such as this to proceed in the way that it does.
A Member who believes there ought to be a revitalization of the railroad system in Canada must vote on the disposition of the coal lands and must at the same time, with the same vote, vote on whether or not the Crowsnest Pass freight rate ought to be changed. Mr. Speaker, in my question to the Minister on Tuesday, June 14, 1 made the Minister aware of the fact that I had received representations from both the Sarcee and Stoney tribal administrations about fiscal problems they are currently experiencing because of the incapacity of departmental officials to consult with band councils prior to forming and implementing policy decisions.
I want to be more specific today. The Sarcee tribal administration cannot agree to the stipulations in the H-12 Circular issued March 15, 1983 by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. As a result of this disagreement, the Band Council has not had access either to its capital funds or to its budget allocation. The Band Council, therefore, is forced to borrow moneys to finance current expenditures. Money urgently needed to provide for the needs of the community is being wasted on the repayment of interest charges on outstanding loans. The moneys that the Band Council is currently using to finance operating costs will run out by June 24, 1983.
The Stoney tribal administration has recently been informed that it is responsible for the repayment of approximately $4 million as a result of an alleged royalty overpayment accumulated over a number of years. Although officials in the

June 16, 1983
Adjournment Debate
Minister's department have been aware of this potential problem since 1979, they did not alert the Band Council to this possibility.
Moreover, when the problem became a reality in 1981, officials from Indian Minerals West unilaterally negotiated with Shell Canada for a recovery process which began on January 1, 1983. At no stage in this process was the band council informed of these developments or consulted as to a possible resolution of the situation.
Although the particulars of these two cases are quite distinct, they both serve to exemplify the extent to which current policies of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development are in direct opposition to statements made by the Minister of the Department. To prove this point, let me quote some of the Minister's statements in his appearance before the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development on June 7, 1983. He said:
As part of my commitment to improving the conditions for native people, I have tried to foster an environment in which their governments have been better able to meet the needs of their constituents.
Despite this commitment, the current funding bypass between the Department and the Sarcee tribal administration will force the Sarcee band to close its administrative offices on June 24 of this year. The Sarcee people face that serious problem, and the federal Government has not taken the time to discuss funding problems with them or to negotiate a reasonable solution to this current impasse. This blatant example of the federal Government's inability to work with Indian governments is particularly surprising to me.
The Minister also said on June 7:
It is important not only to understand what the place of Indian government in Canadian society should be. but also to understand how the Government and Indian people can work together to achieve our objectives for Indian government.
I sincerely hope that what I now see does not exemplify how the Government and Indian people can work together, for if it does there is little hope that Indian people can be optimistic about their future under this Liberal Government.
It may seem that I have been consistently referring back to this one particular speech. I have, but for good reason. The underlying theme of the speech was to emphasize the good will of the Minister and his Department to the Indian people of Canada and to emphasize the importance he places on full negotiation at all times so that Indian people and the federal Government may work in concert for a better future. Yet, whenever a problem arises that needs negotiation to be resolved, the Minister is never available. Instead, the Department simply continues to formulate policy which dramatically affects the daily lives of these people. When this policy is abhorrent to Indian people, they have no option but to submit to it or face bankruptcy. I realize that the Minister's time is limited and that he cannot address every issue personally, but there must be a mechanism in place that will allow Indian people, especially Indian governments, to participate in choices and decisions which affect their future.
Let me refer back to the present situation facing the Stoney Tribal Council. Because of decisions made by Indian Mineral West without consultation with the Stoney tribal administration, the band is now responsible for the repayment of approximately $4 million. In effect, what has happened is that funds allocated to existing projects and payments to band members have been cut to finance the repayment to Shell Canada Limited.
Let us be clear. I am not suggesting that there should be no repayment. Rather, I am suggesting that the Stoney tribal administration should have been party to the negotiation process or at least aware that it was taking place. I do not think that is satisfactory, but they should have known. How can the Minister in good faith continue to say that Indian governments should participate in deciding what their priorities should be when he allows, just to name one example, Indian Minerals West to decide unilaterally upon funding cuts to existing projects to finance the repayment of a debt, for which in all probability they are responsible in the first place.

speakeroldname: Mr. Henri Tousignant (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-FREEZING OF BAND TRUST ACCOUNTS. (B) BAND RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I recognize the interest of the Hon. Member for Wetaski-win (Mr. Schellenberger) in this whole question. But at the same time I cannot accept everything he has just said about the Department, about the Minister and about the Government. I think the Minister and the Department are doing a very fine job. In fact, the Liberal Government has done more for the Indian people of the country than any other Government.
I would like to add to the information which the Minister gave on June 14 in response to two questions by the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger). The first related to the alleged freezing of funds to the Sarcee band. This question related to the involvement or alleged interference by the Department in the affairs of the band and the way it is administered.
I would like to refer the Hon. Member to Circular H-12. He has a copy of it. This circular sets out certain requirements the Minister has to meet in respect to Indian bands' capital funds. These requirements are not onerous and are to some degree flexible to accommodate the different financial systems used by different bands. The requirement that basic information about what money is to be spent for or spent on is fundamental.
In the case of the Sarcee band, it has refused to provide any information about the purpose for which it proposes to use its band capital moneys. All we are asking the Sarcee band to do is to provide us with a simple explanation. It need not be in great detail. When that information has been provided, and I understand that regional officials will be meeting with the Sarcee band to discuss it, then the funds can be released immediately.
June 16, 1983

The question posed by the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin concerning the Stoney band referred to the right of the band to make decisions about its own affairs. The particular case involves the exploitation of mineral resources on the Stoney reserve. This area is the responsibility of the Director of Indian Minerals in Calgary. Past practice has always been to consult with the Indian bands about matters affecting their resources, but the final decision must rest with the director.
The current situation does not involve a question of adjusting oil royalties or in any way changing the nature of the existing agreement. Rather it is a matter of paying the processing charges on natural gas produced on the Stoney reserve which have not been paid since 1979. This amounts to a little over $4 million. These charges are against revenues paid to the band of almost $120 million since 1979.

subtopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-NORTHERN CANADA POWER COMMISSION-COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS. (B) PRICE OF ELECTRICITY SUPPLIED TO PINE POINT MINES
NORTHERN AFFAIRS-NORTHERN CANADA POWER COMMISSION-COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS. (B) PRICE OF ELECTRICITY SUPPLIED TO PINE POINT MINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to register my complete dissatisfaction with the answer given on May 30 by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) to my questions concerning the report of the Parliamentary Subcommittee on the Northern Canada Power Commission, commonly referred to as the Penner Report. This report, Sir, was tabled in the House of Commons or made available on April 7, 1982, some 14 months ago. So far there has been no response to this report by the presumably or so-called responsible Minister. In answering my question on May 30 he only referred to part of the report dealing with possible subsidies. He completely ignored some of the other major recommendations contained in this report, recommendations such as the revocation of the NCPC monopoly in northern Canada. If this were to be revoked, as recommended in the report, a municipality or consumer of power would be able to accept bids from other suppliers rather than be trapped by the Northern Canada Power Commission, not being able to go elsewhere.
There are recommendations contained in this report dealing with better planning mechanisms so as to avoid the many mistakes of the past. One of the most important recommendations deals with the transfer of jurisdiction over power from the federal to the territorial Governments. Nowhere else in Canada, with the exception of a very small part of northern British Columbia, does the Government of Canada get involved in this type of activity. It is something that naturally falls within the jurisdiction of the Province. There is no reason why that should not happen also in northern Canada.
I sometimes wonder what the business of the Government is. Is it the business of the great Government of Canada to run
Adjournment Debate
little 200-kilowatt generators in remote areas? Surely we must be concerned with matters of national importance.
This report recommends a write-off of the great outstanding debt of the corporation, most of which is due to previous mismanagement, especially on capital projects. If we were in a province where power was supplied by private companies, such as Alberta, then the public utilities board of the Province would not allow these excessive capital costs to be rolled into the rate base. The responsibility for cost-over runs would be borne by the shareholders. This is not the case with NCPC.
The report recommends the authority of the Public Utilities Board in the Yukon and Northwest Territories to set the rates of the corporation, the same as for the few private power corporations operating there which are grandfathered in. Nowhere else in Canada is there a situation where the major supplier of power considers itself exempt and aloof from the regulatory process of a public utilities board.
There are a lot of things besides subsidization that should be addressed by the Minister and the Department. When it does come to subsidization, the concept in this report, the ideal or the goal, is that the average price of power in the Territories should approximate the average price of power in the Provinces. I do not think anybody can really disagree with that.
We have to realize the part played by the availability of electricity at reasonable cost in increasing standards of living in undeveloped areas. This should be recognized by the federal Government just as it is by provincial Governments in their rural electrification schemes. It is certainly recognized by Canada in the case of Africa. In 1982 CIDA gave $328 million of Canadian taxpayers' money for electrification schemes. It did not give one nickel to the undeveloped areas of Canada's North.
On many previous occasions have we asked the Minister what he is going to do about this report. When I asked him on November 2 he said he would reply shortly after Christmas. On and on it goes. All he does is commission further studies. He has had a departmental study on the NCPC and now has asked the National Energy Board to again review the matter. The matter has been studied to death. It is time for action and decisions, not further studies. It would appear that the Minister is just incapable of decision. A Member on his side is so frustrated that he said, as quoted in a CBC report dated May 10, 1983:
Keith Penner, the Liberal Member of Parliament who chaired the parliamentary study into NCPC says the federal Government shows a lack of will for not adopting his committee's report and that referring it to the National Energy Board is a delaying tactic to buy more time.
That is also my opinion, the opinion of my constituents and the people in the Northwest Territories and Yukon.

speakeroldname: Mr. Henri Tousignant (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-NORTHERN CANADA POWER COMMISSION-COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS. (B) PRICE OF ELECTRICITY SUPPLIED TO PINE POINT MINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased to be able to comment on the northern energy policy activities which have occurred since the Penner Report was issued about one year ago.

June 16, 1983
Adjournment Debate
The subsidies on electric power to residents of the North outside of the Territory capitals were extended to March, 1984. This program, coupled with the 6 and 5 per cent price guidelines which the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) directed the Northern Canada Power Commission to adopt has saved consumers many millions of dollars in both Yukon and the Northwest Territories. The cost is fully absorbed by the federal Government.
It should be noted that rather than reducing capital spending during a period of reduced demand, the Government has in fact dramatically expanded the expenditures for capital works by the Northern Canada Power Commission. In 1981-82, NCPC capital expenditures were less than $10 million. This was increased to over $40 million in 1982-83, and for the current year is expected to be in excess of $20 million. These expenditures are for hydro investment which should enhance stability in electricity costs over the long-term. They are also a major source for construction employment throughout the North. This is a start on a long-term objective to reduce reliance on diesel powered generating plants.
The Penner Report did not address the issue of how to reduce costs over the long term other than by further expensive Government subsidies to consumers. It is the Government's belief that equitable pricing of energy in the North is necessary. However, this should be coupled with programs that encourage energy conservation and with programs that provide alternative sources of energy. Activities of the federal Government are now concentrated on achieving these objectives.
With respect to the equity of electricity pricing, the Minister requested that the NEB examine the methodologies of rate setting by the Northern Canada Power Commission and assess alternative approaches to regulation of electrical rates. The proposal in the subcommittee report that rate ceilings be fixed, regardless of generating costs, would discourage conservation and delay the development of more cost effective alternative energy sources. The Minister's discussions with the territorial Governments have also confirmed that they too are primarily concerned with the development of local alternate energy sources.
The recent decline in energy demand in the North illustrates the vulnerability of any utility which relies on such a small number of customers for its revenue. In times of acute financial decline, NCPC as a federal Crown corporation can still receive some form of assistance from the federal Government. Any change in ownership of NCPC would alter this support and the financial implications of this are still being examined.

subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION-RULINGS ON RAILWAY BRANCH LINE ABANDONMENTS IN MANITOBA. (B) REQUEST FOR PROTECTION OF SUBDIVISIONS
CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION-RULINGS ON RAILWAY BRANCH LINE ABANDONMENTS IN MANITOBA. (B) REQUEST FOR PROTECTION OF SUBDIVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am very pleased to be able to follow up on a question I raised on Thursday, May 12, with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). I am especially happy since my fiance, Lois Reimer, is
in the gallery tonight to observe me debate this particular question.
I was not very happy on the day the Minister of Transport responded to my question because he mentioned that he was very happy with the record of the Canadian Transport Commission. He said that 88 per cent of the branch line systems we had in the 1930s were currently in place in western Canada. 1 tried to point out to the Minister at that time that 100 per cent of the submissions the CN and CP had made in Manitoba were abandoned. I was very displeased by the Minister's use of those kind of statistics because he certainly did not seem to be grappling with the particular problem.
I have a list of the 18 hearings that have been held in Manitoba by the CTC. The CTC had established a western arm with the sole purpose of assuring that a more sensitive and decentralized hearing would be given to the people in western Canada whose rail lines were being abandoned. We have the record of the CTC hearings regarding the Cabot subdivision, the Boissevain subdivision, the Varcoe subdivision, the Ridge-ville subdivision, the Neepawa subdivision, Pleasant Point subdivision, Carman subdivision as far as the CN is concerned, and the Carman subdivision as far as the CP is concerned, the Wawanesa subdivision, the Hartney subdivision, the Lenore subdivision, the Neepawa subdivision, the Rossburn subdivision, the Lyleton subdivision, the Oakland subdivision, a portion of the Erwood subdivision, the Winnipegosis subdivision and the Inwood subdivision.
I list all these hearings because I think it is important to see what has been happening in western Canada as far as rail line abandonment is concerned, and so the Government can understand the frustration of people in western Canada in constituencies such as Dauphin-Swan River. When a hearing comes to town it is referred to as a three-ring circus. The hoops are set up and constituents are expected to hop through them. The results of the hearing are given out even before the CTC has had an opportunity to read the submissions that have been filed.
I express concern at this time because I think it is high time the Minister looked into the situation and at some of the lines that have been slated for abandonment to ensure that some positive action is taken.
I want to refer to at least two subdivisions which are slated for abandonment in my riding. The Oakland subdivision is slated for abandonment on August 31, 1984. Four Manitoba pool elevators operate on the portion of the line which is up for abandonment, and one of the elevators on this line was upgraded considerably during the Spring of 1982. The grain producers of the area depend very heavily on this line because otherwise they would be faced with insurmountable long hauls for their grain.
I know that the Parliamentary Secretary was not able to be here tonight. When I raised this issue with him and told him that 18 hearings were held, and that 17 of the decisions on
June 16, 1983

those lines were made in favour of the CNR, he expressed doubt. Then he did some independent research, and I have a copy of the results which he passed on to me. The special assistant to the Minister of Transport indicated that in Manitoba it is true that in every application heard, the CTC has decided upon abandonment. This is certainly not justice, Mr. Speaker.
I think it is very important that we look at the issues. The PRAC Commission said that if there were a trucking subsidy or some other way that farmers would be able to cope with the expense of hauling their grain, then perhaps there could be some sort of consideration given to rail line abandonment. I have a letter on file from the Minister which indicates there is no way he would even consider any kind of trucking subsidy, yet the Government allows these types of decisions to be made by the CTC.
The Parliamentary Secretary who is in the House to answer my question tonight is pinch hitting for the Government, but I am sure he will pass my concerns on to the Minister. First of all, why is there an inconsistency? There are lines in Saskatchewan, which do not handle anything like the same amount of grain as handled in those areas in Manitoba that are up for abandonment which have been granted an extension. Why is there this type of inconsistency on the part of the Government in terms of decisions that have been allowed?
When hearings are held, the CNR always makes a representation, and the people who support it are given an opportunity to say what it will cost the CNR or the CPR to maintain the line. But there is never any kind of assistance given by the Government to anyone else, such as PRAC, to indicate the economic impact on the community. Why is there no opportunity for people who have served on PRAC, and people within the Department of Transport such as Mr. Henry Roperts, to make adequate presentations indicating what the economic impact would be on those communities?
I would like to hear answers to these questions. I would like to see these injustices which exist where these railways are being abandoned rectified. I hope there is something in the answer of the Parliamentary Secretary which will at least address some of these questions.

speakeroldname: Mr. Henri Tousignant (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION-RULINGS ON RAILWAY BRANCH LINE ABANDONMENTS IN MANITOBA. (B) REQUEST FOR PROTECTION OF SUBDIVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say first of all that after listening to the Hon. Member, I would be tempted to agree with him. Of course, I too would like to have my own airport. Hon. Members of that
Adjournment Debate
Party are the ones who cry when the deficit goes up. How can they reconcile this?
It seems to me the Hon. Member has two concerns. One relates to what he describes as "the tarnished record of the western division of the CTC". The other is in regard to the hearing process conducted by the Canadian Transport Commission into branch line abandonments.
Dealing first with the second concern, the Hon. Member objects to intervenors going to what he calls a "three ring circus". I am not sure what he would suggest as an alternative to these public hearings. The Railway Act provides for public hearings, and the CTC makes every effort to ensure that all interested parties are heard on abandonment cases. The Act requires that the CTC determine the viability of branch lines and that it consider socioeconomic factors in making its determination. The alternative to this process would be to allow the CTC to make arbitrary decisions, which 1 am sure the Hon. Member does not want.
The Hon. Member's other concern is the record of abandonments in his region, and I recognize and compliment him for having the best interests of his constituents at heart. For the record, Mr. Speaker, since the western division of the CTC was established in July, 1979, there have been eight railway abandonment hearings in Manitoba. Of these eight, there is a decision pending on the Erwood Subdivision for part of the line, and a decision has been made on the Rossburn Subdivision allowing a part of the line to be abandoned on condition that a connecting rail line be constructed to ensure the continuation of adequate service.
I understand that as a result of the Hon. Member's question on May 12 the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis) arranged a meeting between the Hon. Member and a senior official of the Department of Transport to review the Hon. Member's concerns. 1 hope this meeting was useful.
I am sure the Hon. Member realizes that, in addition to the process described earlier, decisions of the CTC can be appealed to the Governor in Council. In conclusion, the Government believes that the process for branch line abandonment is extremely fair, and allows all factors to be carefully considered before a decision is taken.
